# Results — Study 432 (Hull Moving Average) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One recipe — Alan Hull's HMA(16)
slope trend rule turned into a daily **long/flat** timing strategy (long when the HMA is
rising, flat otherwise), entered with one execution lag (position formed on the close of
*t* earns the return of *t+1*), net of one-way costs × NAV — raced against **buy-and-hold**
and against the obvious simpler benchmark, an **SMA(50)** rule and **MACD(12/26/9)**, on a
basket of five liquid US tapes. All series are **total-return** (`auto_adjust=True`); all
Sharpe figures are net and excess-of-cash (rf = 0 here, so net = excess). As-of
**2026-06-13** (last bar 2026-06-12). Headline tape **SPY: n = 8,400 daily bars (~33.3 yr)**.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | Bars | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|---|
| SPY  | 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-12 | 8400 | `e0402ce32988` |
| QQQ  | 1999-03-10 → 2026-06-12 | 6858 | `11b3a1dca229` |
| AAPL | 1980-12-12 → 2026-06-12 | 11467 | `30226e5e62f7` |
| MSFT | 1986-03-13 → 2026-06-12 | 10141 | `e13e0cf0f854` |
| XLE  | 1998-12-22 → 2026-06-12 | 6910 | `8fc9c98d396f` |

## The honest test — SPY, long/flat, net of 2 bps one-way cost

The fair question is not "does the HMA rule make money" (any long-biased rule does in a
33-year bull tape) but "does its **timing** beat just **holding**?" — measured as the daily
**active spread** (strategy net − buy&hold), tested with a Newey-West HAC one-sample *t*.

| Strategy | Sharpe (net) | CAGR (net) | Max DD | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | switches/yr | time in mkt |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **HMA(16) slope** | **0.089** | **0.36%** | −63.7% | **−4.35** | **−5.31** | **32.5** | 58% |
| SMA(50) cross | 0.465 | 4.60% | −43.8% | −2.74 | −3.15 | 17.4 | 69% |
| MACD(12/26/9) | 0.404 | 3.93% | −39.0% | −2.99 | −3.58 | 21.4 | 51% |
| **Buy & hold** | **0.646** | **10.82%** | −55.2% | — | — | 0 | 100% |

- The HMA timing rule **loses to buy-and-hold by 4.35 bps/day** at HAC *t* = **−5.31** —
  statistically significant, on the *wrong* side of zero. Sitting in cash through 42% of a
  bull market is the cost; the HMA's earlier signals do not pay for it.
- It is also **worse than the simpler SMA rule** (Sharpe 0.089 vs 0.465). The "it beats a
  plain moving average" claim is reversed on this tape.
- The gross (cost = 0) spread is **−4.10 bps/day, HAC *t* = −5.01** — costs are *not* the
  killer; the timing itself is the problem.

## "Fewer false signals (whipsaws)?" — the headline claim, measured

The whole selling point of the HMA is that its low lag means **fewer false signals**. We
count position changes (each switch is a round-trip the rule asked for):

| Rule | switches / yr | active spread *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| **HMA(16)** | **32.5** | −5.31 |
| SMA(50) | 17.4 | −3.15 |
| MACD | 21.4 | −3.58 |

The HMA fires **nearly twice as many** position changes as the SMA (32.5 vs 17.4/yr) — the
**opposite** of "fewer whipsaws." Lower lag buys faster reaction *and* more noise-chasing;
on daily equity bars the noise dominates. The claim is busted on its own terms.

## Permutation placebo — is the timing real, or just exposure?

Hold the realised HMA position path's block structure but circularly shift it against
returns (destroying the timing, keeping the turnover and net-long bias), 2,000 draws,
gross spread statistic:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Observed HMA spread | −4.10 bps/day |
| Placebo mean spread | −1.99 bps/day |
| One-sided *p* (placebo ≥ observed) | **1.000** |

Every one of the 2,000 random re-timings beats the real HMA timing. The HMA's *actual*
calls are worse than randomly shuffled calls — the timing carries **negative** information
on this tape, not positive.

## Cost sweep (SPY, HMA long/flat)

| round-trip cost | net Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | 0.145 | −4.10 | −5.01 |
| 1.0 bps | 0.117 | −4.23 | −5.16 |
| 2.0 bps | 0.089 | −4.35 | −5.31 |
| 5.0 bps | 0.005 | −4.74 | −5.76 |
| 10.0 bps | −0.136 | −5.38 | −6.50 |

The spread is negative before costs; there is no break-even cost that rescues it.

## Per-instrument (HMA long/flat, cost = 2 bps)

| Ticker | HMA Sharpe (net) | Buy&hold Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY  | 0.089 | 0.646 | −4.35 | −5.31 |
| QQQ  | 0.107 | 0.519 | −4.82 | −3.66 |
| AAPL | 0.580 | 0.624 | −4.11 | −2.31 |
| MSFT | 0.372 | 0.825 | −7.49 | −6.02 |
| XLE  | 0.148 | 0.438 | −3.87 | −2.52 |

**Five of five** instruments: HMA timing underperforms buy-and-hold, each at HAC *t* ≤ −2.3.
No instrument shows a positive, significant edge.

## Robustness — in/out-of-sample split (SPY, HMA, cost = 2 bps)

| Half | HMA Sharpe (net) | Buy&hold Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| First half (1993–2009) | −0.226 | 0.454 | −4.72 | −3.81 |
| Second half (2009–2026) | 0.457 | 0.882 | −4.10 | −3.71 |

The HMA loses to buy-and-hold in **both** halves; the underperformance is not a
single-regime artefact.

## Long/short variant (SPY, cost = 2 bps, borrow 50 bps/yr)

Flipping to short when the HMA is falling makes it worse: net Sharpe **−0.545**, active
spread **−8.78 bps/day** at HAC *t* = **−5.36**. Shorting an upward-drifting index on a
lagging-by-construction slope signal compounds the loss.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery works when there's a trend to find

On a deterministic synthetic daily tape (`data.synthetic_panel`) with a *planted*
persistent regime-switching trend, the same HMA engine banks the edge — and reads ≈ 0
(slightly negative from turnover drag) when no trend is planted:

| Planted trend `edge` | HMA active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | net Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 (martingale) | −1.88 | −1.62 | 0.26 |
| 0.3 | +3.82 | **+2.64** | 2.14 |
| 0.6 | +19.08 | **+9.29** | 5.41 |
| 1.0 | +41.68 | **+14.39** | 9.31 |

The engine is a faithful trend detector: plant a real trend and the HMA finds it and clears
*t* = 2. The real-tape verdict is therefore a statement about the **market** (daily equity
returns are too noisy at the scale the HMA reacts to) — not a broken harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** HMA timing's active spread vs buy-and-hold is **−4.35 bps/day at HAC
  *t* = −5.31** on SPY (gross *t* = −5.01), negative and significant on all five tapes, in
  both sample halves. The permutation placebo gives *p* = 1.000 — the timing is *worse*
  than random. The lag-free HMA does not add positive timing information on daily US equities.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Even gross, the rule trails buy-and-hold; net of costs and with
  ~32 switches/yr it falls further behind, and the long/short version is outright destructive.
  There is no break-even cost.
- **Cuts false signals? — BUSTED.** The HMA fires **32.5 switches/yr vs the SMA's 17.4** —
  *nearly double* the whipsaws — and underperforms that simpler SMA rule. Lower lag bought
  *more* false signals, not fewer; the central folk claim is reversed on the tape.
